title: Shuffling & hiding
covers: Rail fence, columnar transposition, steganography, product ciphers
learningGoals: You will be able to write and read messages along a Rail Fence zig-zag.
You will be able to perform Columnar Transposition using a numeric key.
You will be able to explain how Steganography hides data inside image pixels.

lessonCards.title: The Rail Fence Zig-Zag
lessonCards.analogy: Writing words down and up along wooden fence rails, then reading off row by row.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Transposition rearranges letter positions without changing identity. Rail fence writes characters diagonally and reads horizontally.

lessonCards.title: Columnar Transposition
lessonCards.analogy: Writing text into columns under a numbered header, then reading out columns by key order.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Characters fill a matrix row by row. Columns are then extracted according to the alphabetical rank of the secret key word.

lessonCards.title: Steganography: Hiding in Plain Sight
lessonCards.analogy: Writing with invisible lemon juice between the lines of a normal shopping list.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Steganography hides the very existence of a secret message by replacing least significant bits (LSBs) of media files.
lessonCards.example: Altering the last bit of RGB pixel values creates color changes invisible to the human eye.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between Cryptography and Steganography?
options: Cryptography scrambles messages; Steganography hides the message's existence
Cryptography uses software; Steganography only uses paper
Steganography is mathematical; Cryptography is not
Cryptography is illegal in modern times
questions.explanation: Cryptography makes data unreadable; steganography conceals the fact that communication is occurring at all.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Cryptography hides content; steganography hides existence.
Both techniques are implemented in modern software.
Both leverage computer science.
Cryptography is standard legal technology.
questions.realWorldExample: Spies have embedded secret text into digital image EXIF tags and low-order audio bits.

questions.prompt: In a 2-rail Rail Fence cipher, how is the plaintext 'ATTACK' written across the rails?
options: Rail 1: A T A, Rail 2: T A K
Rail 1: A T T, Rail 2: A C K
Rail 1: A C, Rail 2: T T A K
Rail 1: K C A, Rail 2: T T A
wrongExplanations: Correct! Letters alternate across top and bottom rails in a zig-zag.
This divides the word in half linearly without zig-zagging.
This uneven division violates standard rail fence progression.
This reversed the characters.
questions.realWorldExample: American Civil War scouts used rail fence ciphers to quickly encode battlefield telegrams.

questions.prompt: In digital image steganography, what does 'LSB insertion' stand for?
options: Least Significant Bit insertion
Longest Secret Byte insertion
Level Security Block insertion
Linear Shift Buffer insertion
questions.explanation: LSB replaces the least significant bit of each color byte (0-255), changing pixel color values by at most 1 unit.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Modifying the least significant bit makes visual color shifts imperceptible to human eyes.
The acronym specifically references bit significance in binary numbers.
Security block is unrelated.
Buffer shifts refer to memory queues.
questions.realWorldExample: A 24-bit 1920x1080 wallpaper image can hide over 700 KB of secret files in its LSB layer.

questions.prompt: What happens to the letter frequency distribution in a pure transposition cipher?
options: Letter frequencies remain 100% identical to the plaintext
Letter frequencies become completely flat like white noise
Vowels vanish from the ciphertext
Every character becomes a random number
questions.explanation: Transposition only rearranges letter positions. The total count of every 'E', 'T', and 'A' remains completely unchanged.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Shuffling characters preserves exact letter frequencies.
Flattened frequencies are the goal of polyalphabetic substitution.
Letters are never removed.
Characters remain letters.
questions.realWorldExample: Cryptanalysts immediately suspect transposition when letter frequencies match ordinary English text.

options: A cipher that combines two or more ciphers in sequence (like substitution + transposition)
A commercial cipher sold in retail stores
A cipher that multiplies numbers without modular division
A cipher designed only for grocery barcodes
questions.explanation: Claude Shannon defined product ciphers as the alternating combination of substitution (confusion) and transposition (diffusion).
wrongExplanations: Correct! Chaining substitution and transposition builds modern block ciphers like DES and AES.
Commercial licensing has nothing to do with it.
Product refers to functional composition.
Barcodes are visual encoding schemes.
questions.realWorldExample: Feistel networks alternate substitution S-boxes with permutation P-boxes to implement product ciphers.

questions.prompt: How can an investigator detect that an image file contains hidden LSB steganography?
options: Statistical chi-square analysis of pixel value frequencies
Zooming in with a magnifying glass
Renaming the file extension to .txt
Checking the file creation date in Windows Explorer
questions.explanation: Natural images have smooth color transitions. Steganography disrupts natural bit pairing, creating detectable statistical anomalies.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Steganalysis tools use statistical frequency tests to detect modified bit distributions.
Human vision cannot detect a 1/255 color shade change.
Renaming file extensions does not analyze internal binary entropy.
File timestamps reflect OS actions.
questions.realWorldExample: StegExpose and Stegdetect are popular forensic tools used by law enforcement to detect hidden payloads.

ashRecap: Transposition shuffles letters like a deck of cards. Steganography hides the secret in plain view so nobody even suspects it's there!
